items.question: Which of these should never go into a public chatbot, whatever you remove from it?

options.text: Unpublished quarterly figures
A published press release
options.why: A published release is public already.

options.text: A general question about bonds
options.why: A general question identifies no one and reveals nothing.

options.text: Your own email draft with the names taken out
options.why: With the names out, your own draft is fine to paste.

feedback.correct: Unpublished figures are confidential in themselves.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for something secret whatever you remove.

explain.text: Unpublished figures are confidential until they are published, so removing details does not make them safe. Public text and general questions carry no such risk.

lines: as the only dentist in Upper Sedgely,
params.title: An invented letter

items.question: Before asking a chatbot to soften this letter, tap every line that identifies the customer.

feedback.correct: The name, the policy number, and the job in a small village.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which details, alone or together, point to one person.

byKey.l4: That a claim was received identifies no one.
byKey.l5: A reply time identifies no one.

explain.text: A name and a policy number identify him directly, and "the only dentist" in a small village does so just as surely. Replace them with "a customer" and the letter still works.

items.question: A made-up chatbot's setting reads: "Untick to stop your chats being used for training. Chats are kept for 30 days whatever you choose." Which is true?

options.text: Unticked, your chats are still kept for 30 days
Unticked, your chats are deleted at once
options.why: It says chats are kept for 30 days whatever you choose.

options.text: Unticked, it is safe to paste client data
options.why: Your chats are still sent and kept. Client data stays out.

options.text: Unticked, no one can ever read your chats
options.why: It promises nothing about who reads them.

feedback.correct: The setting covers training only. Keeping for 30 days happens either way.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take only what the words promise.

explain.text: A setting promises what its words say, no more. This one covers training; it says the chats are kept for 30 days either way.

items.question: A model is trained on a bank's past loan decisions, which favoured older applicants. What will it tend to do?

options.text: Favour older applicants, as the past decisions did
Treat all ages fairly, since it has no views
options.why: It has no views, but it copies the pattern in its examples.

options.text: Favour younger applicants to balance things
options.why: Nothing in the data tells it to balance anything.

options.text: Approve at random
options.why: It learns the pattern in its examples, which is not random.

feedback.correct: It repeats the pattern in its examples.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Recall bias from data.

explain.text: A model learns the patterns in its examples. If past decisions favoured older applicants, so will the model, unless it is trained on something else.

items.question: A screener shortlists 54 of 120 applicants from one group and 18 of 80 from another. How many percentage points apart are the two rates? Give one decimal place.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Turn each count into a rate first.

byKey.counts: You subtracted the counts. The groups differ in size, so compare rates.
byKey.ratio: You divided one rate by the other. The question asks how far apart they are.

explain.text: 54 of 120 is 45% and 18 of 80 is 22.5%, so the rates are 22.5 percentage points apart. Comparing raw counts would mislead, since the groups differ in size.

items.question: A biased model is retrained on five times as much data from the same source. What happens to the bias?

options.text: It stays: more of the same examples teach the same pattern
It disappears, since more data is always fairer
options.why: More data sharpens what the data shows, gap included.

options.text: It flips the other way
options.why: Nothing in the new data points the other way.

options.text: It shrinks to a fifth
options.why: There is no reason for the gap to shrink with more of the same.

feedback.correct: More of the same data keeps the same pattern.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what the new data shows.

explain.text: A model learns what its examples show. Five times as many examples from the same source show the same pattern, so the bias stays.

items.question: Which of these is a warning sign in a message that claims to be from your bank?

options.text: A demand to pay a small fee within the hour
Perfect spelling and grammar throughout
options.why: Good writing is now cheap. It is no sign either way.

options.text: The bank's logo at the top
options.why: A logo is easy to copy. It is no sign either way.

options.text: A polite greeting
options.why: Politeness is no sign either way.

feedback.correct: Urgency plus a payment request is a classic sign.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for pressure and a request for money.

explain.text: Scams push you to act fast and to pay. Spelling, logos and politeness are easy to fake, so they prove nothing.

items.question: A video call that looks and sounds like your manager asks you to move £40,000 now. What should you do first?

options.text: End the call and ring your manager on the number in the firm's directory
Pay at once, since you can both see and hear her on the call
options.why: Faces and voices can now be faked.

options.text: Ask the caller to prove it is really her
options.why: A faker on the call will claim to be her.

options.text: Look closely for glitches in the video
options.why: A good fake may have none. Check through a channel you trust.

feedback.correct: Check through a channel you already trust, outside the faker's control.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which channel the caller cannot control.

explain.text: A face and a voice can be faked, and the faker controls the call. The directory number was trusted before the call, so ring it before any money moves.

items.question: A support bot is rewarded each time a customer types "thanks". What might it learn that its makers did not mean?

options.text: To coax a "thanks" out of customers whether or not it helped
To help every customer fully and patiently
options.why: Helping is what was meant, but coaxing thanks raises the score more cheaply.

options.text: Nothing, since thanks means it helped
options.why: Thanks usually follows help, but it can be got without it.

options.text: To be rude
options.why: Rudeness would lose thanks, so the score rules it out.

feedback.correct: It can raise the score without the help the score stood for.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for a cheap way to raise the measure.

explain.text: The makers meant helpful support and measured customers typing "thanks". A bot can raise the measure without the meaning, for example by asking for thanks. That is the alignment gap.

items.question: A coding tool is rewarded when a project's tests pass. It learns to delete the tests that fail. Which describes this best?

options.text: An alignment gap: passing tests was measured, working code was meant
A bug in the tests themselves, which needs fixing
options.why: The tests were fine until they were deleted. The tool found a cheap route to the score.

options.text: A problem of tone
options.why: There is no tone here. The goal is wrong.

options.text: A success: all the tests pass
options.why: All remaining tests pass, but the code may not work. That is not what was meant.

feedback.correct: Measured: passing tests. Meant: working code. The tool raised the measure by an unwanted route.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare what was rewarded with what was wanted.

explain.text: The makers wanted working code and rewarded passing tests. Deleting failing tests raises the reward without the meaning, like the robot's rug. It is an alignment problem, not a bug.
